record.paper_title: Open problems in graph theory. II: On the achromatic number of a graph
record.context_brief: Polynomial-time classes for tree achromatic number
record.original_question: For which classes of finite trees can the achromatic number be determined in polynomial time, where the achromatic number of a graph G is the maximum integer K for which G has a complete K-coloring, and a complete K-coloring is a vertex coloring with colors {1,2,...,K} in which adjacent vertices receive different colors and every pair of distinct colors appears on the endpoints of at least one edge?

evidence.quote: The maximum integer K for which a graph G has a complete K-coloring is called the achromatic number of G. For many years it was not known whether the achromatic number of a tree can be found in polynomial time. It now remains to determine for what classes of trees can the achromatic number be determined in polynomial time.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph. A complete K-coloring of G is a function c : V → {1, 2, …, K} such that:
(i) c(u) ≠ c(v) whenever {u, v} ∈ E (proper coloring), and
(ii) for every pair of distinct colors i, j ∈ {1, …, K}, there exists at least one edge {u, v} ∈ E with {c(u), c(v)} = {i, j}.
The achromatic number ψ(G) is the largest integer K for which G admits a complete K-coloring.

It is known that computing ψ(G) is NP-hard in general, and remains NP-hard when G is restricted to be a tree. Characterize the classes of finite trees for which the achromatic number can be determined by a polynomial-time algorithm. In particular, identify natural structural classes 𝒞 of trees (for example, defined by bounds on degree, diameter, depth, caterpillar-like structure, or similar parameters) such that there exists an algorithm computing ψ(T) for every T ∈ 𝒞 in time polynomial in |V(T)|.
artifact.status_search_result: The achromatic number problem is NP-hard for general trees. Polynomial-time algorithms are known for some restricted tree classes, notably trees of bounded maximum degree (Chaudhary & Vishwanathan; Bodlaender; et al.), and for complements of trees. The broader question of characterizing all tree classes admitting polynomial-time algorithms remains an active area, so the problem is partially solved.

status_evidence.claim: Bounded-degree trees admit polynomial-time computation of the achromatic number.

status_evidence.snippet: Computing the achromatic number is NP-hard; it remains NP-hard for trees.
status_evidence.claim: The general tree case is NP-hard, motivating the search for tractable subclasses.
